name: Detective Sergeant Luis Becerra
equipment: Heavy overcoat, brown gabardine, over a brown suit his wife chose
.38 revolver (Colt Official Police, department issue), 6 rounds loaded, on his belt
Nightstick, in the car, and a blackjack he never uses in his desk drawer
Pump shotgun (Winchester Model 12, department issue), 5 rounds loaded, in the trunk of his unmarked Ford
A steel vest in the Ford's trunk, for raids, which he hates
Detective sergeant's shield and Port Calloway PD identification card
Notebook, pencils and a fountain pen his daughter gave him
A Speed Graphic camera from the property room, borrowed, signed out properly
Car: 1950 Ford Custom sedan, unmarked, with a police radio and a spotlight
A rosary in his coat pocket and a photograph of his wife and three children in his hat
features: Seen Worse (Ex-Service origin: advantage on saves against being frightened and against the Shaken condition; the first time each combat he is hit by a firearm, he keeps his reaction and any readied action)

The Badge (Cop: while he carries his shield and the department has not pulled it, he has lawful authority: he can enter a crime scene, demand identification, commandeer a telephone or a car in an emergency and detain a person for questioning; it also has a chain of command, and Lt. Dunleavy is at the top of his)
Academy Training: Riot Squad (Cop: +1 AC while wearing medium armor; he wears the steel vest only on raids)
Collar (Cop, 2nd level: when he hits with a melee attack, a bonus action to grapple; he can handcuff a grappled creature as an action with no check)

Assignment: Detective (Cop, 3rd level: proficient in Forensics; once per long rest, examining a scene, the GM tells him which of the people he knows had the best opportunity, though not necessarily the motive)
Ability Score Improvement (Cop, 4th level: +1 Strength, +1 Wisdom)
Extra Attack (Cop, 5th level: he attacks twice when he takes the Attack action)

Old Outfit (Veteran background: Marines who were at Guadalcanal will do anything for each other, and there are more of them in Port Calloway than anyone would think: a mechanic, a coroner's assistant, a ferry purser, a man at the phone company)

personality.traits: I am patient, polite, and tired, and I write everything down. I call everyone sir or ma'am, including the people I am arresting. I go to Mass at seven on Sundays and lie to my priest about my job.
personality.ideals: The badge is a promise to people who cannot afford a lawyer. When a cop breaks it, he breaks it for every cop.
personality.bonds: My wife, Carmen, and our three kids in a little house on Beacon Street with a mortgage I will be paying until 1971. And the men I came home with from the Pacific, and the ones I didn't.
personality.flaws: I have known for two years that Ray Dunleavy is bent and I have kept my head down because of that mortgage. I am ashamed of it every day. When I finally move, I may move too far.

appearance: A compact, solid man of thirty-nine with a square brown face, a neat black moustache, tired dark eyes and thick black hair going grey at the sides. He dresses like a bank clerk in a brown suit and overcoat and walks with a slight limp from a Japanese grenade on Guadalcanal. He smokes Luckies and stops himself halfway through each one.
backstory: Luis Becerra was born in the Port Calloway barrio by the rail yards, the son of a section-gang foreman, and joined the Marines in 1940 because the recruiting sergeant was the first white man who ever called him sir. He fought on Guadalcanal and Peleliu, came home with a limp and a Silver Star, and joined the police in 1946 on the GI Bill, one of the first Mexican-American officers in the city. He made detective in 1949 on merit and has been stuck at sergeant ever since because he will not take envelopes and everyone knows it. He works Homicide under Lt. Ray Dunleavy, whom he despises, and he has watched Dunleavy write up three deaths as natural causes that were not. He has done nothing about it, because he has a family and because there is no one in the department to take it to. This week Dunleavy has asked for the DA's security detail, which he has never done for anything, and has told Becerra to keep an eye on some private detectives. Becerra has decided to keep an eye on Dunleavy instead.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Becerra is the party's honest cop, the one door into the police that Dunleavy does not control. Introduce him in pa-scenario-001 in the Hall of Justice corridor, warning the party and offering help in the same breath. He becomes an ally in pa-scenario-002 or 003 when the party shows him something he cannot ignore (Lindqvist's death, the pencil note in Dahl's ledger, Dunleavy at the Pelican). In pa-scenario-003 he gives them the security rota in a parked car. In pa-scenario-004 he can put himself backstage at the Regent, arrest Teague or Dunleavy, and swear a complaint for Special Agent Hale. He is a companion who brings The Badge: he can open doors the party cannot, and he is bound by rules the party is not. Make that friction real.
dmNotes.voice: Quiet, courteous, precise, with an occasional Spanish word when he is angry or tender. Never swears. Says 'sir' in a way that can mean anything from respect to contempt. When he is frightened he gets more formal.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: keep the DA alive, because it is his job, whatever the DA is. Secondary: find out what Dunleavy is doing and stop it, without losing his badge or his house. Tertiary: be able to look at his kids.
dmNotes.secrets: He kept a copy of the coroner's notes on two of the three deaths Dunleavy wrote up as natural, in a shoebox in his garage, with the dates and the names of the Larch Hill men each dead man had crossed. It is not proof of anything on its own. With the party's evidence, it is a pattern, and Special Agent Hale will want it. Second, smaller secret: he applied to the FBI in 1947 and was turned down without explanation; he suspects why, and he will find Hale hard to like at first.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: wary, then loyal. He thinks private detectives are men who could not make it as cops, and is delighted to be wrong. Toward Walt Embry: respect; he knows why Walt left the force, or thinks he does. Toward Dunleavy: icy correctness. Toward Sloane: a cop's duty to a man he would not let into his house. Toward Nora Kessling: protective, as he would be of his own daughter in ten years.
